Order, positivity and distributional limits

Reconstructed by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), Ultra reasoning effort, October 2026. The earlier edition was written by GPT-6.1 Sol (OpenAI), Ultra reasoning effort. Original lesson exposition and exercises: CC0. The separately credited programme prerequisites retain their own licences.

A distribution is controlled by finitely many derivatives on each fixed compact region. The required number can grow as the region changes. Positivity removes this derivative cost: a positive distribution is a measure, and its convergence reaches continuous compact tests. Without positivity, large opposite masses can cancel on smooth tests while diverging on continuous ones.

We supply the test-space, support and finite-net arguments below. The included functional foundations prove complex Hahn–Banach, the complete-metric Baire theorem and completeness of fixed-support smooth test spaces. The included positive-measure construction proves the exact Riesz representation and regularity used here. Scalar calculus, cutoffs and integration have their full proofs in the three accompanying foundation selections listed after the solutions. These are available proof texts, not external citations in place of proofs.

Proposition 1.1 (the sequential test). A linear form is a distribution if and only if it sends every sequence tending to zero in to a scalar sequence tending to zero.

Distributions are locally finite derivatives of measures

The included functional foundations prove this exact complex Hahn–Banach statement: a bounded complex-linear functional on any subspace of any complex normed space extends with the same norm. The subspace need not be closed and the ambient space need not be complete. Theorem M of the measure prerequisite proves positive Riesz representation on , together with the necessary local-finiteness, regularity and uniqueness statements. We use its convention that a locally finite complex measure is specified consistently on relatively compact regions; it need not assign a finite complex value to the whole unbounded space.

Let consist of continuous complex functions vanishing at infinity, meaning that is compact for each . Its norm is . Such a function is bounded: outside the compact set for it is less than one, and on that compact it has a finite maximum. Compactly supported continuous functions are dense in this norm. Indeed, multiply by a cutoff equal to one on , giving error at most .

Corollary 3.3 (order zero is precisely a measure). Order-zero distributions are exactly locally finite complex Radon measures. The measure is unique and acts continuously on .

Positivity forces order zero

A linear form is positive if is real and nonnegative for every real nonnegative smooth test. No continuity is assumed in this definition.

Theorem 4.1 (positive forms are measures). Every positive linear form on is an order-zero distribution. Its continuous-test extension is represented by a unique positive Radon measure.

Proof. Fix compact and a nonnegative compact smooth cutoff on . For real , both and are nonnegative. Subtracting such functions also shows that is real on every real test. Positivity therefore gives

A zero value satisfies the same bound. This proves order zero. Proposition 1.2 supplies the continuous-test extension. For a nonnegative continuous test, convolution with the nonnegative mollifier used there preserves nonnegativity. Passing to the limit shows that the extension is positive. Theorem M now gives its positive Radon measure and uniqueness.

This measure may have infinite total mass. Conversely a derivative of a point mass is not positive: take a bump equal to one near zero and supported in , multiply it by or , and pair its derivative at zero. The two nonnegative tests give opposite signs.

Exercises

  1. Increasing order — advanced. On the real line, define . Prove that it is a distribution but has no finite order valid on the whole line. Exhibit tests supported near one integer that defeat any proposed order bound.
  2. A dipole limit — intermediate. For (5.4), compute the distributional limit and total variation. Evaluate it on a continuous test equal to near zero, and prove that the limiting distribution has order exactly one.
  3. Mass leaving compact sets — foundation. Prove that on , although the total masses diverge. Find a bounded continuous test for which the pairings do not tend to zero.
  4. Two representations of zero — intermediate. Express the derivative of in the first form of (3.2). Then use a nonzero and to construct a nonzero measure family representing the zero distribution, and check the signs.
  5. Uniform continuous tests — advanced. Under Theorem 5.2, suppose a family has common compact support, uniformly bounded values and a common modulus of continuity after zero extension. Prove convergence is uniform over , using one finite net for the whole family.

Complete solutions

Solution 1. A compact set meets only finitely many positive integers. On , the pairing is consequently a finite sum, bounded by . This is a local finite-order estimate, and is zero when the index set is empty.

If a global order existed, choose an integer and a compact interval around containing no other integer. Let , where is a compact smooth cutoff equal to one near zero; then . For small , the tests

are supported in that interval. Their derivatives through degree have uniform bounds for , whereas . This contradicts the proposed bound on one fixed compact set.

Solution 2. The fundamental-theorem calculation after (5.4) gives the limit . The variation of each two-point measure is : partitioning into its two atoms attains this value, and the triangle inequality bounds every other partition by it. The continuous test has value for large .

The derivative of a point mass has order at most one by its defining action. It cannot have order zero. Choose compactly supported and smooth with ; the functions have bounded supremum and common compact support for , while the absolute value of their pairing with is . Thus the order is exactly one, as it is for its negative.

Solution 3. Each compact support misses the point eventually, making its pairing exactly zero for all sufficiently large . The total mass is nevertheless . The constant function one is bounded and continuous and has pairing , so it supplies the requested failure outside the compact-test class.

Solution 4. Ordinary integration by parts gives . Thus the first form of (3.2) uses , with other measures zero. The second form has , preserving the sign. To represent zero, use , , and all other measures zero. Their first-form pairing is . These compact measures form a nonzero family when , whereas the all-zero family represents the same distribution. If desired, their Radon character follows by splitting the real and imaginary continuous densities into positive and negative parts and applying (M12) to Lebesgue measure.

Solution 5. Enclose the common support in a finite cube and use a finite grid. The common modulus of continuity makes the change from any point to its nearest grid point uniformly small for every function in the family. Partition the bounded complex range into finitely many small-diameter sets at the grid points and choose one member from each nonempty finite signature class. The same argument as (T3), with the common modulus in place of the Lipschitz bound, gives a finite -net in supremum norm, with centers in the family. All supports are still in the original compact set.

Choose a compact neighborhood and cutoff as in (5.3), giving a common bound for the measures and their limit. If , then

Each of the finitely many centers converges by (5.2). Taking the supremum and then the limit superior bounds it by ; let . The single finite net makes this estimate uniform over the entire family.
